notes.summary: Time, speed and distance is built on one rule: distance = speed × time. Trains, boats, races and circular tracks are all this rule with relative speed added. SSC asks 1–2 questions in Tier 1 and 1–2 in Tier 2, often on average speed, trains and boats.

concepts.title: The one formula
concepts.body:
Distance = Speed × Time. So Speed = Distance ÷ Time and Time = Distance ÷ Speed.

Keep the units matching: km with hours, metres with seconds.

  • km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18. 72 km/h = 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s.
  • m/s to km/h: multiply by 18/5. 15 m/s = 54 km/h.
  • Minutes to hours: divide by 60. 45 minutes = 3/4 hour.

concepts.title: Proportion rules (the fastest tool)
concepts.body:
• Same distance: speed and time are inversely proportional. Speed ratio 3 : 4 means time ratio 4 : 3.
  • Same time: distance is proportional to speed.
  • Same speed: distance is proportional to time.

Example: a car at 60 km/h takes 5 hours. At 75 km/h the same trip takes 5 × 60/75 = 4 hours.

concepts.title: Speed change and time change
concepts.body:
When the speed changes by a fixed amount and the time changes by a fixed amount, write:

D/(s − x) − D/s = extra time (or D/s − D/(s + x) = time saved).

Then test the options; it is usually faster than solving the quadratic.

Example: 384 km. If speed falls by 16 km/h, the trip takes 2 hours more. Try s = 64: 384/48 − 384/64 = 8 − 6 = 2. So the speed is 64 km/h.

concepts.title: Late and early arrival
concepts.body:
If a person walks at a/b of his usual speed, he takes b/a of his usual time. The extra time = (b/a − 1) × usual time.

Example: at 3/4 of usual speed he is 18 minutes late. Extra = 1/3 of usual time = 18, so usual time = 54 minutes.

With two speeds S1 and S2 (late at one, early at the other):

Distance = S1S2/(S2 − S1) × (total time difference)

Example: at 40 km/h he is 10 minutes late, at 50 km/h 5 minutes early. Difference = 15 min = 1/4 h. D = 40 × 50/10 × 1/4 = 50 km.

concepts.title: Average speed
concepts.body:
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time. It is not the simple average of the speeds unless the times are equal.

CaseAverage speed
Equal distances at x and y2xy/(x + y)
Equal distances at x, y and z3xyz/(xy + yz + zx)
Equal times at x and y(x + y)/2

Example: 40 km/h going and 60 km/h returning: 2 × 40 × 60/100 = 48 km/h.

Example: three equal parts at 20, 30 and 60 km/h: 3 × 20 × 30 × 60/(600 + 1800 + 1200) = 30 km/h.

concepts.title: Relative speed
concepts.body:
• Moving in opposite directions: relative speed = a + b.
  • Moving in the same direction: relative speed = a − b.

Time to meet (towards each other) = gap ÷ (a + b). Time to catch up (same direction) = gap ÷ (a − b).

Example: A walks at 4 km/h. 4 hours later B cycles after him at 10 km/h. Gap = 16 km, relative speed = 6 km/h, so B catches A after 16/6 = 8/3 hours, at 10 × 8/3 ≈ 26.67 km from the start.

concepts.title: After crossing each other
concepts.body:
Two people start at the same time from P and Q towards each other. After meeting, they take t1 and t2 hours to reach the other end. Then:

S1 : S2 = √t2 : √t1

Example: after meeting, A takes 9 hours and B 4 hours. Speed ratio A : B = √4 : √9 = 2 : 3.

Also, time to meet = √(t1 × t2) = 6 hours here.

concepts.title: Trains
concepts.body:
The distance a train covers while crossing something = its own length + the length of the other object.

CrossingDistanceSpeed used
Pole, man, treetrain lengthtrain speed
Platform, bridge, tunneltrain + platformtrain speed
Man walkingtrain lengthrelative speed
Another trainsum of both lengthsrelative speed

Example: trains of 120 m and 180 m run in opposite directions at 40 and 50 km/h. Relative speed = 90 km/h = 25 m/s. Time = 300/25 = 12 s.

concepts.title: Boats and streams
concepts.body:
Let u = speed of the boat in still water and v = speed of the stream.

  • Downstream (with the river): D = u + v.
  • Upstream (against the river): U = u − v.
  • u = (D + U)/2 and v = (D − U)/2.

Example: downstream 18 km/h and upstream 12 km/h. Boat = 15 km/h, stream = 3 km/h.

Round trip of distance d: total time = d/(u + v) + d/(u − v). If a man takes twice as long upstream as downstream, then u + v = 2(u − v), so u = 3v.

concepts.title: Races
concepts.body:
• A beats B by x metres: when A finishes, B is x metres behind.
  • A beats B by t seconds: B finishes t seconds after A.
  • A gives B a start of x metres: B runs x metres less.
  • Dead heat: both finish together.

If A beats B by x metres or t seconds, then B covers x metres in t seconds, so B’s speed = x/t.

Chain example: in a 100 m race A beats B by 20 m and B beats C by 25 m. When A runs 100, B runs 80 and C runs 80 × 75/100 = 60. A beats C by 40 m.

concepts.title: Circular tracks
concepts.body:
Let the track length be L.

  • First meeting anywhere = L ÷ relative speed (add speeds for opposite directions, subtract for the same direction).
  • First meeting at the starting point = LCM of the times each takes for one lap.

Example: 200 m track, speeds 18 km/h (5 m/s) and 24 km/h (20/3 m/s). Lap times: 40 s and 30 s. They meet at the start after LCM(40, 30) = 120 s.

concepts.title: Stoppage time
concepts.body:
If the average speed is S1 without stoppages and S2 with stoppages, the train stops for

(S1 − S2)/S1 × 60 minutes per hour.

Example: 50 km/h without and 40 km/h with stoppages. Stop time = 10/50 × 60 = 12 minutes per hour.

varieties.name: Speed, time and distance basics
varieties.how: Write time for each part as distance ÷ speed. Add the times and set the total equal to the given time. Convert units first.

example.q: Vipin travels one-third of a journey at 30 km/h and the rest at 40 km/h. The whole journey takes 12 hours. What is the total distance?

varieties.name: Average speed
varieties.how: Total distance ÷ total time. For two equal distances use 2xy/(x + y); for equal times use (x + y)/2.

example.q: Reshma covers 45 km at 15 km/h, 80 km at 40 km/h and 6 km at 2 km/h. What is her average speed, correct to 2 decimal places?

varieties.name: Change in speed changes time
varieties.how: Write the time difference as D/(slow speed) − D/(fast speed) = difference. Try the options instead of solving the quadratic.

example.q: A truck covers 384 km at a certain speed. If the speed is reduced by 16 km/h, it takes 2 hours more. What is 75% of its original speed?

varieties.name: Late and early arrival
varieties.how: At a/b of usual speed, time becomes b/a of usual. The extra (b/a − 1) of usual time equals the minutes late. For two speeds use D = S<sub>1</sub>S<sub>2</sub>/(S<sub>2</sub> − S<sub>1</sub>) × time difference.

example.q: Walking at 3/4 of his usual speed, a man reaches office 18 minutes late. What is his usual time?
steps: Speed is 3/4, so time is 4/3 of usual.
Extra time = 1/3 of usual time = 18 minutes.

varieties.name: Meeting and chasing
varieties.how: Find the gap between them when both are moving. Divide by the sum of speeds (towards each other) or the difference (chasing).

example.q: A starts walking at 4 km/h. After 4 hours, B starts cycling from the same point in the same direction at 10 km/h. How far from the start will B catch A?

varieties.name: Trains crossing
varieties.how: Distance = sum of the lengths involved. Use the train’s own speed for still objects and relative speed for moving ones. Convert km/h to m/s with 5/18.

example.q: A train crosses a pole in 15 seconds and a platform 100 m long in 25 seconds. Find the length and speed of the train.
steps: The extra 10 seconds are spent covering the 100 m platform.

varieties.name: Boats and streams
varieties.how: Find downstream speed D and upstream speed U from distance ÷ time. Boat speed = (D + U)/2, stream speed = (D − U)/2.

example.q: A boat covers 35 km downstream in 2 hours and the same distance upstream in 7 hours. Find the speed of the boat in still water.

varieties.name: Circular track
varieties.how: First meeting = track length ÷ relative speed. Meeting at the starting point = LCM of the lap times.

example.q: On a 2200 m circular track, two cyclists start from the same point in opposite directions at 20 km/h and 16 km/h. When will they first meet?
steps: Opposite directions: relative speed = 36 km/h = 10 m/s.

varieties.name: Races
varieties.how: If A beats B by x metres or t seconds, B runs x metres in t seconds. For chains, scale the distances: when A runs 100, B runs (100 − x) and so on.

example.q: In a 1 km race, A beats B by 50 m or 10 seconds. How long does A take to finish?
steps: B covers 50 m in 10 s, so B’s speed = 5 m/s.
B takes 1000/5 = 200 s for the race.

varieties.name: Stoppage time
varieties.how: Stop time per hour = (speed without stops − speed with stops) ÷ speed without stops × 60 minutes.

example.q: A train averages 50 km/h without stoppages and 40 km/h with stoppages. How many minutes does it stop per hour?
steps: Time to cover 10 km at 50 km/h = 10/50 h.

tips: Convert units before anything else: km/h × 5/18 gives m/s.
For the same distance, speed ratio a : b means time ratio b : a.
For equal distances, average speed is 2xy/(x + y), always a little less than the simple average.
In speed-change questions, plug the options in instead of solving a quadratic.
Boat speed = (down + up)/2, stream speed = (down − up)/2.
Meeting at the starting point on a circular track: take the LCM of lap times.
For stoppage time per hour: (difference of speeds ÷ faster speed) × 60.
traps: Average speed is not (x + y)/2 when distances are equal.
When a train crosses a platform, add the platform length to the train length.
Use relative speed when the other object also moves (a man walking, another train).
“Beats by 10 seconds” is about the loser’s time, not the winner’s.
Check whether the answer is wanted in km/h or m/s, and minutes or hours.

formulas.name: Two speeds, late and early
formulas.expr: D = S1 × S2/(S2 − S1) × time difference

questions.q: A speed of 72 km/h is equal to:
A car covers 360 km in 4 hours 30 minutes. What is its speed?
A train 150 m long is running at 54 km/h. How long will it take to cross a platform 300 m long?
A boat goes downstream at 18 km/h and upstream at 12 km/h. What is the speed of the stream?
Two trains 120 m and 180 m long are running in opposite directions at 40 km/h and 50 km/h. In how many seconds will they cross each other?
questions.solution:
Relative speed = 40 + 50 = 90 km/h = 90 × 5/18 = 25 m/s.
Distance = 120 + 180 = 300 m.
Time = 300/25 = 12 s.

questions.q: A man goes from A to B at 40 km/h and returns from B to A at 60 km/h. What is his average speed for the whole journey?
questions.solution:
Equal distances, so average speed = 2xy/(x + y).
= 2 × 40 × 60 / 100 = 48 km/h.
